planting.note: Plant grafted or rooted container specimens in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, siting them out of strong wind, which can tatter the broad leaflets and scorch the white leaf margins.

directions: Plant in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun and wind, both of which can scorch the creamy-white leaf margins. This RHS Award of Garden Merit selection carries the same huge, twice-compound, spine-stemmed architecture as the species but each leaflet is edged in irregular white variegation, making it a prized specimen for shaded borders and woodland gardens. It suckers less vigorously than the green-leaved species and reverted all-green shoots should be pruned out promptly at the base to preserve the variegation. Propagation is by grafting or removal of variegated root cuttings, since seedlings do not come true.

planting.note: Plant grafted or rooted container specimens in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to light dappled shade for the best gold leaf-margin color.

directions: Plant in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to light dappled shade; too much sun bleaches the gold margins, while deep shade fades them toward plain green. Another RHS Award of Garden Merit sport of the Japanese angelica tree, this cultivar opens with soft yellow leaflet margins in spring that mature to creamy gold through summer, set off by the huge, prickly-stemmed, twice-compound framework typical of the species and topped by large white flower panicles in late summer. Cut out any all-green reverted suckers at ground level as soon as they appear to keep the planting true to type. Give it a sheltered site out of strong wind to protect the large leaves from tearing.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in early spring into sharply drained, sandy or rocky, acidic soil; established colonies also self-sow into open, disturbed ground.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, sandy or rocky acidic soil in open woodland, clearings, or partial shade at a woodland edge; unlike its shade-loving relatives, bristly sarsaparilla thrives in leaner, more open sites and tolerates dry, infertile ground poorly suited to most other Aralia. The lower stem is distinctively armed with fine bristles rather than stout spines, and plants form low colonial patches topped by rounded clusters of small white flowers in summer, followed by dark purple-black berries used by birds and historically by foragers alongside the related wild sarsaparilla. It spreads slowly by rhizome and is well suited to naturalizing a sandy barren, pine clearing, or rock garden edge rather than a moist shade bed. Division in spring is the reliable way to propagate named colonies, since seed germination is slow and erratic.
